1108.name: Independent and confident cooking
1108.description: This unit introduces pupils to working in a different environment, learning new skills and procedures, and using a range of equipment. The focus is on establishing hygiene and safety procedures, and the food skills measuring, peeling, cutting and using the hob. Sensory work is undertaken.
1108.why: Learning how to prepare and cook food safely in unfamiliar environments builds confidence, engagement and adherence to procedures for health. Transitioning from Year 6, pupils' prior food experiences progress in terms of food skill accuracy, and range of ingredients and equipment used, via the threads of Food preparation and cooking, Food hygiene and safety, and Sensory evaluation. This lays the foundation for more complex and independent cooking, and investigating The science of food during Year 7. In Year 8, Food preparation and cooking progresses, with a focus on technique and proficiency.

Pupils will be able to get ready to cook, so that they are safe and hygienic.
Pupils will be able to demonstrate the 'bridge hold' and 'claw grip' techniques when cutting, slicing and dicing.
Pupils will know that the hob is used for boiling and frying food in pans.
Pupils will be able to describe the sensory attributes of a dish.

1110.name: The Eatwell Guide: meals and diets
1110.description: In this unit pupils use the Eatwell Guide, the 8 tips for healthy eating, and portion guidance to plan healthy meals and evaluate diets. They also use food labels to help make better food and drink choices.
1110.why: Throughout life, a variety of factors affect the food and drink we choose, some of which are personal preferences, while others are cultural, linked to occasion, and where we are and who we are with. Building on previous work of Consumer awareness and Food culture threads in Year 6, pupils critique food choices and suggest alternatives. Looking forward to Year 8, pupils address the influence of ingredient availability, cooking technique and equipment on healthy eating, and explore the source and function of nutrients.
prior: Pupils are able to talk about the Eatwell Guide.
Pupils can name the main food groups of the Eatwell Guide.
Pupils will know the names of the main nutrients needed for health.
Pupils are able to explain how meals could be modified for health.

1111.name: Food origins
1111.description: Pupils describe the origins of different foods, identifying how they have been produced, processed and sold. Food labels are used to investigate ingredient origins. Pupils cook two dishes, investigating ingredient source, as well as functional properties.
1111.why: Understanding the origin of ingredients allows informed decisions to be made, such as location, farming practice or ethics. Food labels and other information indicates origins. This builds on from previous work in Year 5 around Food origins and provenance, and safe and edible food in Year 6. In Year 8, pupils investigate Sustainability and further their learning around Consumer awareness factors, such as food choice, suggesting practical strategies that could be implemented for healthier and more sustainable diets.
prior: Pupils can sort foods into plant and animal origin, and name some 'farm to fork' chain steps.
Pupils can name the stages of producing some foods.
Pupils can explain why and how some food is processed.
Pupils will know that labels provide a variety of information about a food.

1112.name: Informed food choices
1112.description: This unit develops pupils' knowledge of food choice, and how occasion and location can have an influence. Food skills and nutrition understanding are further developed through practical work, and the use of components are explored.
1112.why: Throughout life, a variety of factors affect the food and drink we choose, some of which are personal preferences, while others are cultural, linked to occasion, and where we are and who we are with. Building on previous work around Food culture and Consumer awareness in Year 6, pupils critique choices and suggest alternatives. Looking forward to Year 8, pupils address the influence of ingredient availability, cuisine, cooking technique, and equipment on food choice locally and around the world.
prior: Pupils will know that different people eat different foods.
Pupils can list some factors that affect food choice.
Pupils will know that we eat different food on different occasions and celebrations.
Pupils can identify the key nutrients provided by a selection of foods.

1113.name: Cooking techniques and proficiency
1113.description: This unit extends pupils' cooking techniques, focusing on their food skill proficiency. Pupils develop food skills and apply their nutrition understanding. Recipe modification is undertaken, through nutritional analysis, and the functional properties of key ingredients are analysed.
1113.why: Being proficient with a range of food skills enables us to prepare and cook more complex recipes, extending our repertoire. This confidence also enables us to successfully modify recipes for health, variety and preference. Progressing from Year 7, through the thread of Food preparation and cooking, pupils continue to refine their food skills, embedding The science of food, and Sensory evaluation learning, leading to more independent work. In Year 9 the focus is on greater precision and accuracy in preparation and cooking, and the exploration of food science in practice.

Pupils can wash-up and wipe work surfaces, to prevent bacteria from spreading.
Pupils can set up and undertake different sensory evaluation tests.

1114.name: Energy and nutrients: source and function
1114.description: Pupils describe the source and function of macro and micro nutrients, as well as fibre and water in the diet for health. The concept of energy balance is reviewed, and pupils undertake nutritional analysis of recipes.
1114.why: Energy, nutrients, fibre and water are needed in different amounts, are from a range of sources, and have specific functions for health. This builds on previous Eatwell Guide learning, food groups and proportions in Year 8, enabling pupils to apply nutritional knowledge when making healthier choices and modifying recipes, through linking food source and function. In Year 9, pupils explore changing nutritional needs throughout life, as well as allergies and health conditions.
prior: Pupils know that the Eatwell Guide depicts the food and drinks required for a healthy, balanced diet.

Pupils can name the food source of some nutrients.
Pupils know that a diet is the food and drink that a person usually eats over a period of time.
Pupils know that portion sizes are an amount of food eaten.

1115.name: More sustainable diets
1115.description: In this unit pupils identify ways in which a diet can be healthier and more sustainable. Pupils suggest practical ways in which a range of strategies could be implemented. Through cooking two dishes, pupils apply this learning, giving them tools to adapt recipes in the future.
1115.why: There are a number of strategies that can be employed to create healthier, more sustainable diets. Practical strategies allow consumers to make a difference to their health and the planet, such as including more fruit and vegetables, and having a greater diversity of protein sources. This builds on the threads Food origins and provenance, and Sustainability. In Year 9, pupils investigate global food challenges, further exploring the principles of how diets can be more sustainable.
prior: Pupils can describe the food origins of ingredients in dishes and meals.
Pupils can name the origin of foods grown, reared or caught for consumption.
Pupils can talk about how food is sourced, processed and sold in different ways, helping to ensure it is edible and safe to eat.
Pupils can describe the healthy eating messages of the Eatwell Guide and list its food groups.

1116.name: Local food to worldwide cuisine
1116.description: This unit focuses on the wide range of cuisines, ingredients, cooking techniques and equipment that are used around the world. Pupils explore food imports, food produced in the UK, and food waste. They cook two dishes to highlight cuisine differences, undertaking different types of evaluation.
1116.why: Cuisines are a set of cooking traditions and techniques, associated with a specific culture, region and ingredients. This recognition provides insight into cooking and recipe choice, fulfilling consumer tastes for more international cuisines, while honouring traditional UK dishes. This work builds on previous learning in Year 7 around the threads of Food culture, Consumer awareness, and Food origins and provenance. During Year 9, pupils further reflect on food culture, and how food forms part of our identity, heritage, tradition, custom and celebration.
prior: Pupils can identify and explain the different factors that affect food choice.
Pupils can list a range of factors that affect food choice.
Pupils know that communities have different needs, based on age, nutritional need, preferences, culture, faith and belief.
Pupils can describe a range of different ingredients used to flavour dishes from around the world.
Pupils can explain how food is part of different customs, traditions and celebrations.

1117.name: Accurate and precise cooking
1117.description: Through three recipes, the emphasis of this unit is on accurate and precise use of a range of food skills, and independent working. High standards of food safety are embedded, and pupils modify recipes for health and explore food science in action and the cost of ingredients.
1117.why: Cooking independently provides pupils with the confidence and transferable skills to cook at home and apply their learning life long. Accuracy and precision are refined, based on previous work in Years 7 and 8 of becoming more proficient in a range of food skills, and employing strategies to keep safe and hygienic. Pupils continue to secure and fine-tune their food skills in Year 9, preparing, cooking and presenting a range of dishes, while embedding food safety and hygiene, and deepening the application of food science.
prior: Pupils can maintain high standards of good personal hygiene and food safety, explaining its rationale.
Pupils can use a wide range of equipment and demonstrate a variety of food skills.
Pupils can use healthy eating messages to suggest changes to the ingredients and cooking method in a recipe.
Pupils can talk about yeast producing carbon dioxide, which helps bread to rise.
Pupils know that home-cooked dishes can be compared to shop-bought for a number of factors.

1118.name: Health and dietary needs
1118.description: In this unit pupils explore key nutritional needs throughout life, and allergies, food labelling, portion size and health conditions. They plan dishes and menus, and describe how diets can be changed for health to meet the needs of different groups of people.
1118.why: Dietary and nutritional needs change throughout life, and being able to plan diets for the needs of different people is important to minimise any potential consequences of poor diet. This builds on work in Year 8 around the name, source and function of different nutrients, and the application of healthy eating guidelines. Going forward, pupils will have the knowledge, skills and strategies to plan diets and make meals for themselves and others, now and in the future.
prior: Pupils can describe the energy and nutrients provided by food and drinks, and their important functions for health.
Pupils can modify recipes and cooking methods to help meet current healthy eating messages.
Pupils can use the Eatwell Guide, food portion and size, and 8 tips to evaluate and justify healthier changes to a diet.
Pupils can read food labels, choosing those lower in fat, salt and sugars.
Pupils will know that people have an allergy to specific ingredients, such as wheat flour, nuts and milk.

1119.name: Global food challenges
1119.description: This unit investigates the pressure on food systems, caused by climate change and a growing population. Pupils critique these challenges and explore principles of more sustainable diets, balancing the needs of the planet and human health. Practical work reinforces these principles in action.
1119.why: Climate change and a growing population present real challenges to our global food systems. Examining these challenges enables us to be better informed about the decisions we make as consumers. The application of previous learning in Year 8, around strategies to create healthier and more sustainable diets, and consider the needs of people, are built upon and expanded. This learning provides pupils with a firm foundation to be better informed consumers, making good decisions based on their needs and beliefs.
prior: Pupil can identify ways diets can be healthier and more sustainable.
Pupils can explain why the Eatwell Guide has a 32% lower environmental footprint than the current national diet.
Pupils can modify recipes and diets to be healthier and more sustainable.

1121.name: Food culture and custom
1121.description: This unit concludes pupils' food learning journey in Key Stage 3. Pupils reflect on food culture, looking at how food is deeply rooted in identity, heritage, tradition, custom and celebration. Two dishes are prepared, highlighting different cooking styles and histories, and traceability is explored.
1121.why: Throughout history, the food that has been eaten has been defined by a number of factors, such as location, food availability, cultural heritage, custom and tradition. Examining food culture enables us to have greater awareness of diversity, and appreciate its role and place in society. This progresses work from Year 8 around international cuisine and cultural factors affecting food choice. In the future, pupils will continue to recognise the importance and significance of food in their lives, not just for health, but for greater human connection and joy.
prior: Pupils can describe a wide range of cuisines, ingredients, cooking techniques and equipment used around the world.

2816.belief: Everyone needs the same amount, or portion, of food.
2816.statement: Everyone needs the same amount, or portion, of food.
2816.correction: Everyone needs slightly different amounts of food, depending on their age and activity levels.

5742.belief: Potatoes can form part of our 5 A DAY.
5742.statement: Potatoes can form part of our 5 A DAY.
5742.correction: Potatoes do not count towards our 5 A DAY. They are a starchy carbohydrate in the Eatwell Guide.

3073.belief: Most of the food we eat is produced in the UK.
3073.statement: Most of the food we eat is produced in the UK.
3073.correction: About 54% of the food on our plates is produced in the UK, the rest is imported from other countries.

10260.statement: Some might think that shortcrust pastry works best when the butter (or baking fat) and water used are warm, not cold.
10260.correction: Make sure the butter or baking fat is cold, and that pupils use cold water, this helps to ensure that the pastry works better. When rubbing-in the fat to the flour, use fingertips only, as less heat is passed from the hands to the fat.

5142.belief: The 'all-in-one' method produces poor results, as the ingredients are not creamed together and/or whisked.
5142.statement: The 'all-in-one' method produces poor results, as the ingredients are not creamed together and/or whisked.
5142.correction: The 'all-in-one method' is a quicker cake making method, producing good results. Using self-raising flour and mixing throughly ensure the cakes rise well.

4368.belief: We only make conscious food choices about what food we buy, cook and eat, based on a range of factors.
4368.statement: We only make conscious food choices about what food we buy, cook and eat, based on a range of factors.
4368.correction: We make conscious and unconscious food choices about the food we buy, cook and eat.

537.belief: Baking tins do not need to be greased and/or lined.
537.statement: Baking tins do not need to be greased and/or lined.
537.correction: It is important to grease (with oil) or line (with greaseproof paper) a baking tin, as this acts as a barrier and prevents the food from sticking.

8956.belief: Rice should be stirred when cooked, so ensure it is covered in liquid.
8956.statement: Rice should be stirred when cooked, so ensure it is covered in liquid.
8956.correction: It is best not to stir most rice dishes. Stirring breaks the rice and releases starch, making the rice feel mushy and ‘over cooked’. Risotto is stirred though, as the starch helps the dish have a creamy texture.

570.belief: Beans can count as many portions towards 5 A DAY, depending on the number of portions eaten.
570.statement: Beans can count as many portions towards 5 A DAY, depending on the number of portions eaten.
570.correction: Beans count as a maximum of one portion of 5 A DAY, no matter how much is eaten.

1739.belief: Coeliac disease is caused by a reaction to gluten in wheat flour only.
1739.statement: Coeliac disease is caused by a reaction to gluten in wheat flour only.
1739.correction: Coeliac disease is caused by a reaction to gluten (a protein), which is found in flours from wheat, barley and rye.

9025.belief: A roux sauce can have all the liquid (milk) added at the same time, and whisked occasionally.
9025.statement: A roux sauce can have all the liquid (milk) added at the same time, and whisked occasionally.
9025.correction: A roux sauce must have the liquid (milk) added gradually, and the sauce should be whisked continually to prevent lumps.

2570.belief: We should eat less starchy foods, as these are 'fattening' in the diet and provide little else.
2570.statement: We should eat less starchy foods, as these are 'fattening' in the diet and provide little else.
2570.correction: Starchy foods should make up just over a third of the diet, as they are an important source of energy, fibre and micronutrients.

126.belief: An adequate intake of micronutrients is possible by always eating the same types of foods.
126.statement: An adequate intake of micronutrients is possible by always eating the same types of foods.
126.correction: To ensure an adequate intake of micronutrients, it is important to have a varied diet. This is because different foods provide different types and amounts of vitamins and minerals.

2572.belief: The Eatwell Guide recommends a plant-rich, non-meat diet.
2572.statement: The Eatwell Guide recommends a plant-rich, non-meat diet.
2572.correction: The Eatwell Guide recommends that we should have a plant-rich diet and reduce the amount of red and processed meat, if we eat too much.

5554.belief: Plant-rich means that we should not eat meat or dairy foods for healthier and more sustainable diets.
5554.statement: Plant-rich means that we should not eat meat or dairy foods for healthier and more sustainable diets.
5554.correction: It is not necessary to cut out meat or dairy from our diet completely for healthier and more sustainable diets. Follow the Eatwell Guide: have plenty of fruit and veg; diversify sources of protein; and limit foods high in fat, salt and sugars.

4392.belief: When making two recipes at the same time, you should cook them separately in order. This takes longer, but the recipes are made well.
4392.statement: When making two recipes at the same time, you should cook them separately in order. This takes longer, but the recipes are made well.
4392.correction: When making two dishes at the same time, read both recipes first to decide which order to complete the steps in each recipe - this is known as dovetailing. Dovetailing results in a better use of time, where tasks fit together easily.

4094.belief: Leftovers will still be safe to eat after 3 - 4 days, as they still look good.
4094.statement: Leftovers will still be safe to eat after 3 - 4 days, as they still look good.
4094.correction: Leftovers should be used within 48 hours from when it was made (24 hours for rice dishes). Longer periods of time increase the risk of food poisoning bacteria multiplying.

10517.belief: The UK produces all of its own food.
10517.statement: The UK produces all of its own food.
10517.correction: The UK produces 58% of the food it consumes, 42% is imported from other countries. This is due to season, cost, climate, and to add variety to the diet.

9560.belief: A sponge and cake are the same.
9560.statement: A sponge and cake are the same.
9560.correction: Often the term ‘sponge’ and ‘cake’ are used interchangeably. However, sponges are traditionally made from eggs, flour and sugar (no butter), e.g. Swiss roll, and cakes are made from eggs, flour, sugar and butter, e.g. lemon drizzle cake.

3079.belief: If a food is placed in the fridge, there is no need for it to be covered or placed in a container, as the fridge is a cold and safe storage area.
3079.statement: If a food is placed in the fridge, there is no need for it to be covered or placed in a container, as the fridge is a cold and safe storage area.
3079.correction: All food placed in the fridge must be covered or placed in a container to prevent cross contamination with other foods, preventing food poisoning. It also helps to stop the food drying out.

8793.belief: Recipes cannot be modified for different budgets, as the stated ingredients must always be used.
8793.statement: Recipes cannot be modified for different budgets, as the stated ingredients must always be used.
8793.correction: Recipes can be modified for different budgets, using a number of strategies, such as comparing costs, buying own-brand items, and using seasonal fruit and vegetables.

3056.belief: Any flour can be used to make a bread-like dough.
3056.statement: Any flour can be used to make a bread-like dough.
3056.correction: Although most flours will produce a dough, a strong flour is recommended as it is high in protein (gluten), which is needed to help trap the air and form the bread structure when baked.

3077.belief: Food hygiene is only about being clean when preparing, cooking and storing food.
3077.statement: Food hygiene is only about being clean when preparing, cooking and storing food.
3077.correction: Food hygiene is necessary in order to prepare and cook food which is safe to eat. It involves the 4Cs: cleaning (including personal hygiene), cooking, chilling and preventing cross-contamination.

2339.belief: Dietary Reference Values (DRVs), nutritional requirements, are intended for individual healthy people.
2339.statement: Dietary Reference Values (DRVs), nutritional requirements, are intended for individual healthy people.
2339.correction: Dietary Reference Values (DRVs), nutritional requirements, are intended for different groups of healthy people. They are a series of estimates of the energy and nutrients required.

5129.belief: There is one form of malnutrition, intakes of energy and/or nutrients being below what is required.
5129.statement: There is one form of malnutrition, intakes of energy and/or nutrients being below what is required.
5129.correction: There are two forms of malnutrition: undernutrition (intakes below what is required) and overnutrition (intakes above what is required).

10368.belief: Traditional fried falafel is healthy, as it is made from chickpeas.
10368.statement: Traditional fried falafel is healthy, as it is made from chickpeas.
10368.correction: While the chickpeas are a healthy choice, falafel is usually deep-fried, so less healthy. Alternative cooking methods could be used which use less oil, such as grilling, baking, or air-frying.

665.belief: Biodiversity is not important in growing food, only the plants growing are important.
665.statement: Biodiversity is not important in growing food, only the plants growing are important.
665.correction: Biodiversity is important in growing food by promoting a healthy and balanced ecosystem, e.g. encouraging insects and birds to live near fields can help keep pests under control.

2571.belief: Eating a limited range of fish is sustainable, as fewer species are caught.
2571.statement: Eating a limited range of fish is sustainable, as fewer species are caught.
2571.correction: 80% of the fish we eat comes from five species, which puts pressure on these fish stocks. We should eat a wider variety of fish to ensure more sustainable supplies.

3067.belief: Following the Eatwell Guide is only about eating more healthily.
3067.statement: Following the Eatwell Guide is only about eating more healthily.
3067.correction: While following the Eatwell Guide will help people eat more healthily, it also has a 32% lower environmental footprint, compared to the current national diet, so can help us eat more sustainably too.

2137.belief: Cultural appropriation is just appreciation and admiration of other cultures.
2137.statement: Cultural appropriation is just appreciation and admiration of other cultures.
2137.correction: Cultural appropriation can be the unacknowledged or inappropriate adoption or use of elements of a minority culture by members of the dominant culture, often in a way that is disrespectful, stereotypical, or exploitative.

9132.correction: While its name may sound Scottish, the Scotch egg has origins in 1738 London (a snack for travellers), India (nargisi kofta), and Yorkshire (a fish version).

2414.belief: The dishes we cook, eat and serve, along with our food experiences, have stayed the same over time.
2414.statement: The dishes we cook, eat and serve, along with our food experiences, have stayed the same over time.
2414.correction: The dishes we cook, eat and serve, along with our food experiences, continue to evolve (change over time) due to a variety of factors, such as history, culture, social media and health.
